rv.q: Nothing Can Take You from the Hand of God is miraculous, an exceptional piece of tenderness and solace whose wisdom and insight elevates its form.
For all its intellectual rigor and metatheatrical pyrotechnics, Nothing Can Take You from the Hand of God is most remarkable for its emotional honesty.

Jen Tullock's solo show, written with Frank Winters and inspired by Tullock's upbringing in an evangelical church, stealthily, brilliantly complicates a trope that has become gospel in the theater, television, and publishing industries.
Too much enjoyment rules from fast start to fast finish, the foremost Tullock’s indefatigable performance.
It's a heady piece of work, a solo show teeming with personalities and equipped with its own running commentary.

There are times when the technology threatens to overtake the human stories–the clashing voices, in both the writing and Tullock's sharply etched performance, are strong enough to do the work, and I think I would have found the multimedia effects more compelling if used slightly more sparingly.
I left Nothing Can Take You from the Hand of God impressed with Tullock's energy and vigor, and baffled about exactly what the hell happened.
As a portrait of growing up queer in an evangelical household with psychologically abusive parents, the play succeeds completely.

Tullock gives a tour-de-force performance, quickly changing accents and body language while also adjusting several onstage looping stations and small cameras that record real-time visuals of her that are projected onto screens around her, as if each character contains their own multitudes, going beyond stereotypes.

cn.t: Critics praise Jen Tullock's hyperkinetic solo show as a mesmerizing examination of memory, faith, and truth, lauding her tour-de-force performance and the production's inventive multimedia staging under Jared Mezzocchi's direction.
